findings.problem: The section turns the 21 CFR 1305.17(e) deeming rule into a storage-segregation rule. It says an electronic Form 222 copy kept in the pharmacy's general document store and pulled by keyword search fails the test, and retrieval_prompts[6] keys 'Separately' as the word that such an arrangement fails.
findings.rationale: 1305.17(e) deems electronic copies separately maintained if they are 'readily retrievable separately from all other records'. 'Readily retrievable' is a defined term (21 CFR 1300.01(b)): records kept by electronic or mechanized systems so that they can be separated out from all other records in a reasonable time. The test is retrieval, not physical segregation. An electronic Form 222 copy sitting in a shared document store meets it if the system can separate the Forms 222 out in reasonable time, and 1305.13(a) expressly lets the purchaser's copy be electronic. The section's categorical answer is wrong, and it undercuts the accurate statements in quick_review[9], forms_records[3] and comparison_tables[0].rows[5].

results.summary: MINOR_EDIT, severity Medium. Checked against current eCFR text: the seven 1305.03 exceptions, the 60-day window with the Defense Supply Center exception (1305.13(b),(f); 1305.22(e),(h)), defect handling (1305.15; 1305.25(d)), lost forms and the in-transmission carve-out (1305.16; 1305.26), preservation (1305.17; 1305.27), the CSOS data fields (1305.21) and the two-business-day supplier report (1305.29) are all stated accurately. This also contradicts released question MA-Q-0438 (key B). (2) The paper-route purchaser receipt record in 1305.13(e) is omitted. (3) The paper supplier's month-end copy to DEA and its retention of the original are missing from the comparison tables. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 16 adopts the federal order-form requirement, so the empty ma_vs_federal field does not distort Massachusetts law.

findings.problem: The entry says the section's inventory and retention duties are 'entirely federal' and that Massachusetts contributes only registration. A candidate applying the section to Massachusetts facts would conclude that Massachusetts imposes no inventory or record duties of its own.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 15 makes the federal record-keeping and inventory requirements Massachusetts duties of every registrant and adds the Board's additional rules for a retail drug business. The Board has added inventory events that the section never flags. At a change of Manager of Record, the pharmacy must attest to an inventory of all Schedule II-V substances and of the Schedule VI substances reportable to the prescription monitoring program (247 CMR 6.10(2)(a)). On closure or transfer of ownership, a complete inventory is taken on the transfer date (247 CMR 6.14(2)(a)). Schedule II stock is kept on a perpetual inventory that is reconciled at least every ten days (247 CMR 9.21(8)). Calling these duties entirely federal hides that the Massachusetts inventory can reach PMP-reportable Schedule VI drugs and invites wrong answers to Massachusetts inventory questions.

findings.rationale: Federal law is also premises-based. A separate DEA registration is required for each principal place of business (21 CFR 1301.12(a)), and 1304.11(a) requires a separate inventory for each registered location. findings.problem: The section reduces the Massachusetts theft-or-loss route to the Manager of Record's duty to investigate and to report 'in accordance with federal and state requirements', and concludes that the state rule 'points back at 21 CFR 1301.74(c) rather than replacing it'. It never teaches the Massachusetts reports that run alongside the DEA report.
findings.rationale: A Massachusetts Drug Store pharmacy must also report a theft or loss of a significant amount of controlled substances to the Board. It does so by submitting a copy of the 'Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance' and DEA Form 106 within seven days, and it must also comply, where applicable, with DEA, Department and state and local police requirements (247 CMR 20.03(7)). Whenever a person registered to dispense must file a DEA Form 106, M.G.L. c. 94C, § 15 requires it to file a copy at the same time with the police department of the city or town where the theft or loss occurred and with the state police. Where the operator is itself a Department registrant, such as a hospital, 105 CMR 700.008 adds a 24-hour report to the Drug Control Program. A candidate who applied this section to Massachusetts facts would report only to DEA.

findings.problem: Throughout, the section grounds the pharmacy's federal theft-or-loss duty in 21 CFR 1301.74(c), which is the paragraph for non-practitioners. A pharmacy is a practitioner (21 U.S.C. 802(21)), and its duty is in 21 CFR 1301.76(b).
findings.rationale: 1301.76(b) has the same one-business-day written notice, the same 45-day Form 106 through the secure network application and the same six significance factors. It does not have the 1301.74(c) sentence about substances that are later recovered, or the allocation of in-transit losses to the supplier. For practitioners, 1301.76(d) makes the retail pharmacy responsible for in-transit losses when it contracts the carrier that collects filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy. exceptions[4]'s statement that the rule 'allocates in-transit losses away from the receiving registrant' is therefore not true of pharmacies generally. The clocks are right; the governing provision, and the reach of the sentences imported from 1301.74(c), are not.

findings.problem: The section applies 105 CMR 700.005(B), including the employment bar in (B)(2), to 'a Massachusetts pharmacy' as the employer.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 700.005(B) binds 'applicants and registrants', and 105 CMR 700.001 defines Registrant as a person 'registered by the Department'. Pharmacies are registered by the Board, not by DPH: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 7(a) requires every pharmacy to register with the Board; 247 CMR 11.01 authorizes the Board to issue that registration; and 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1) confines DPH registration to persons 'other than a registered retail drug business or wholesale druggist'. 247 CMR 9.21(12) confirms the split by sending only institutional sterile compounding pharmacies to 105 CMR 700.000 for security. The bar therefore reaches a pharmacy only where its operator holds a Department registration, such as a hospital. It does not reach the Board-licensed pharmacy in worked_examples[2]. Released question MA-Q-0384 rests on the same premise and should be reviewed together with this section.

findings.problem: The personnel-security material leaves out the federal bar that does bind every DEA-registered pharmacy, 21 CFR 1301.76(a).
findings.rationale: Under 1301.76(a) a registrant may not employ, as an agent or employee with access to controlled substances, anyone convicted of a felony relating to controlled substances, or anyone who at any time had a DEA application denied, had a DEA registration revoked, or surrendered one for cause. The federal bar differs from the Massachusetts rule in both directions. It adds felony drug convictions and surrenders for cause, but it applies only to employees with access, so restricting access does matter federally. worked_examples[2].steps[4] says the opposite ('narrowing his duties does not answer it'). A candidate would also miss the felony-conviction bar entirely.

findings.problem: The section says 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) is written without a waiver and that 'there is no exception to find'.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 700.140 lets the Commissioner waive one or more requirements of 105 CMR 700.000. The Commissioner must find undue hardship, no jeopardy to health or safety, and acceptable compensating measures, and the registrant must supply written documentation. That is a waiver route for a Department registrant, and it rests on the same compensating measures the section dismisses as dead ends. At the federal level, 21 CFR 1307.03 lets any person ask DEA for an exception to a provision of the chapter, including 1301.76(a).

results.summary: MAJOR_REWRITE, severity High. The 247 CMR 9.21 material matches the 12/6/2024 text: storage arrangements, alarm, cameras with 14-day and two-year video retention, the barrier, direct delivery, the Schedule II perpetual inventory with its ten-day reconciliation, the entry and adjustment rules, and 9.21(9)-(12). The disposal material (1317.05(a)-(b), 1317.15, 1317.90, 1317.95, the 1300.05 definition of non-retrievable, 1304.21(e)) is also accurate. The theft-or-loss and personnel parts cannot be published as they stand. (1) The section omits the Massachusetts reports that run alongside the DEA report: the seven-day Board filing with a copy of the Form 106 (247 CMR 20.03(7)) and the simultaneous copies to the local and state police (M.G.L. c. 94C, § 15). It tells the candidate instead that the state rule merely points back at the federal one. (2) It grounds the pharmacy's federal duty in the non-practitioner paragraph, 1301.74(c), instead of 1301.76(b). (3) It applies the DPH employment bar in 105 CMR 700.005(B) to a Board-registered pharmacy, which is not a registrant as that regulation defines the term. It omits the federal bar in 1301.76(a), which does apply, and it denies the waiver route in 105 CMR 700.140. (4) It never names the DEA Form 222 for Schedule II transfers to a reverse distributor or for returns. All seven mapped questions can be answered from the section and none is contradicted, but MA-Q-0384 shares the 105 CMR 700.005(B) actor premise.
